Messages.Author: Daneel
Messages.Body:
On Wed, 02 Feb 2005 19:21:39 -0500, Peter D Bakija <pd...@lightlink.com>
wrote:

> jeff_kuta wrote:
>
>> I can easily see situations where a player would intentionally violate
>> the "play to win" doctrine just to win a side prize.
>
> Yeah, I suppose that is possible, but do such, like, wacky door prizes
> invalidate sanctioning?

Well, sanctioning has very little effect on the tournament AFAIK except
for the fact that player ratings are updated (of which we keep very
little track of, honestly).

Technically though it may change the tournament atmosphere. I've seen
people play decks that aimed at collecting one of the prizes. In doing
so their decks may not have been sufficiently optimizted with respect
to actually ousting, winning and such. Of course it's quite hard to
tell as I don't know every Hungarian player, and lots of new faces show
up at these tournaments - someone might've just been a n00bie anyway.

As for the rules - I dunno. They may or may not have a restriction on
prizing, I guess it's a yes (I presume that prizes must support
achievement with respect to winning, like you can't (ad absurdum) do a
tournament where the finalists get nothing, the non-finalists get a
booster and those with 0 VPs get two boosters).

--
Bye,

Daneel

Well, Zsolt is kind of a border-line case, him being fluent in
Hungarian... ;)

Anyway, I'm in no way affiliated with the Bookstore or its owners, but I
think that the restriction on the participation was due to the fact that
the Bookstore considers this event to be a form of advertising. They
invest in providing a tournament with remarkable prizes, attracting
players to it whom may later end up visiting the Bookstore regularly. In
this sense a local player is far more likely to do so than a foreigner...
I know that other events (even those supported by the Bookstore) are open
to foreigners as well, but this event was heavily sponsored. It helps
newbies integrate into the regular gaming community, and it also promotes
the Bookstore. I'm sure noone at the Bookstore has anything against
foreigners, it's just that they are immensely less likely to become
regulars at the shop...

--
Bye,

Daneel

Messages.Body:
"Daneel" <dan...@eposta.hu> wrote in message

>

> Technically though it may change the tournament atmosphere. I've seen
> people play decks that aimed at collecting one of the prizes. In doing
> so their decks may not have been sufficiently optimizted with respect
> to actually ousting, winning and such.

...

> As for the rules - I dunno. They may or may not have a restriction on

> prizing, I guess it's a yes...

I think the argument against using incentives like that would be pretty
apparent: they're out-of-game considerations, similar in nature to (for
instance) one player making a deal with another player to give him a rare
card in exchange for allowing himself to be ousted. Of course, I realize
the point is completely different and no one's trying to do anything evil
but out-of-game considerations are out-of-game considerations, even when
the tournament organizers are involved.

Of course, whether small or gag prizes would make much difference in the
real world is another matter. I just know I'd be a bit annoyed if my
game position took a hit only because someone was trying to earn a gag
prize for some chuckles. (Just my attitude about such things, I guess.)

Fred

Messages.Author: Frederick Scott
Messages.Body:
"Gregory Stuart Pettigrew" <ethe...@sidehack.sat.gweep.net> wrote in message
news:2005020310...@sidehack.sat.gweep.net...


Actually, I don't see the difference between deckbuilding and the game-time
playing of the cards: both are activities in which you're expected to try
to win. You do get broad latitude about which style you choose in pursuit
of that goal (and the same can be said of card play here, too), but either
way, winning is expected to be the goal.

So speaking of "optimized" vs. "non-optimized" decks in this context makes
no sense. Every deck should "optimized" to win - in the manner of style in
which the player intends it to win and to the best of the player's abilities
given his available resources. With all these caveats, no one usually
questions another player's deckbuilding choices. But I think it's still
wrong (at least in standard tournaments) to build a deck geared towards
earning some alternate prize in lieu of building one geared to winning games
and winning the tournament.

Fred
